## 7.1 Why This Gets Its Own Section

Part 3, §3.5 already described the data extraction and entity resolution step as a procedure. This section treats the *same step* as an engineering design problem in its own right, because it is the most labor-intensive and the most cost-sensitive part of the entire project. Two concerns drive this design:

1. **Token consciousness.** Every call to a large language model (LLM — a model like Claude that processes and generates text) consumes "tokens" (the discrete chunks of text the model reads and writes, roughly three to four characters of English text each), and providers bill per token. A poorly designed extraction pipeline can burn through tokens redundantly — for example, by re-sending the same long instructions on every single call — without the researcher noticing until the bill arrives.
2. **Workflow efficiency toward semi-automation.** "Semi-automated" means the pipeline should require a human only at points where human judgment is genuinely necessary (verifying a contested fact, resolving an ambiguous name), and should run unattended everywhere else (parsing, formatting, first-pass classification). This is a deliberate middle ground between full manual transcription (Tier 1 in Part 4) and a fully autonomous pipeline (which would be inappropriate here, because §3.5 already established that human verification of extracted facts is a non-negotiable scientific integrity requirement, not merely a nice-to-have).

The architecture below is organized around four engineering levers, each independently confirmed as effective for this exact kind of workload — bulk, offline, repetitive document-extraction processing — by current LLM provider documentation and third-party benchmarking.

## 7.2 Lever 1 — Model Routing (Use the Cheapest Model That Can Do the Job)

**The principle:** Not every extraction task requires the most capable (and most expensive) model. Pricing data confirm a roughly fifteen-to-fifty-times cost difference between budget-tier and flagship-tier models, and the most effective architectures explicitly reserve flagship models for complex reasoning while routing simple classification and extraction tasks to cheaper models.

**Applied to this project, the task breakdown is:**

| Task | Complexity | Recommended model tier | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pulling a clean number/name/date out of a sentence with an unambiguous pattern (e.g., "TTES No. 12 was released in 1981") | Low | Budget tier (e.g., Claude Haiku) | This is pattern recognition, not reasoning. A schema with fewer than ten flat fields is, according to current provider guidance, nearly as accurately handled by a budget-tier model as a flagship one, at a fraction of the cost. |
| Resolving which of two conflicting parentage claims is more likely correct, or noticing a subtle naming collision between two sources | Medium–High | Mid/flagship tier (e.g., Claude Sonnet) | This requires comparing two pieces of context against each other and exercising judgment, which is exactly the kind of task that justifies the higher per-token cost of a more capable model. |
| Drafting prose for the eventual manuscript (Step 8, §3.9) | High | Flagship tier | Writing quality and nuance benefit most from the most capable model; this task happens rarely (a handful of times total), so its higher per-call cost barely affects the overall budget. |

**[RECOMMENDATION]** Build the extraction pipeline so the *model name is a configuration parameter, not something hardcoded inside the prompt logic*. This means the same extraction code can be pointed at a cheap model for a first pass and re-pointed at a more capable model only for the subset of records that the first pass flags as low-confidence or ambiguous — a "cascade" pattern that applies the expensive model only where it is actually needed.

## 7.3 Lever 2 — Structured Output (Guarantee the Shape of the Answer, Don't Ask Nicely For It)

**The principle:** Asking a model in plain English to "please return JSON" is unreliable — providers' own documentation acknowledges that prompting alone can yield JSON occasionally wrapped in markdown formatting or accompanied by unwanted conversational text. The reliable alternative is to force the model to use a defined "tool" (in Claude's API, a tool is a function-like schema the developer defines; the model's response is then constrained to match that schema exactly, rather than being free-form text). When the developer sets `tool_choice` to force the model to call one specific tool, the model's output is guaranteed to be valid, schema-conforming data — a pattern providers explicitly recommend as the standard for any production data extraction workload.

**Applied to this project:** Define one tool per node type in the schema from §3.4 (one for `Cultivar`, one for `Species`, one for `ParentGermplasm`, and so on). Each tool's schema should mirror exactly the node properties already defined in §3.4 — meaning the schema design work from Part 3 is directly reusable here, not separate work. Every field description inside the tool schema should be written carefully, since the description text is itself part of what the model reads and uses to decide what to extract — better field descriptions measurably produce better extractions.

**Concrete mechanical benefit:** This eliminates an entire category of wasted tokens and wasted time — failed parsing attempts that require a retry. A single failed JSON-parsing attempt that triggers a retry costs more in tokens than the small schema overhead added by using structured tool calls in the first place.

## 7.4 Lever 3 — Batch Processing (Don't Pay for Speed You Don't Need)

**The principle:** Anthropic's Batch API allows asynchronous submission of large volumes of requests, processed within a 24-hour window, at a flat 50% discount on both input and output tokens, for every Claude model, with no minimum volume threshold required to unlock the discount. The only requirement is that the workload tolerate a delay of minutes to hours rather than needing an instant reply — which is exactly the nature of document extraction, since no human is sitting and waiting for each individual record to be extracted in real time.

**Applied to this project:** None of the steps in §3.5 require an instant response. The entire first-pass extraction step (pulling structured records out of every saved source) should be submitted as a single batch job: every paper, every TRES web page excerpt, bundled into one submission, rather than triggered one document at a time through an interactive chat interface. This single architectural choice halves the cost of the entire extraction phase before any other optimization is applied.

## 7.5 Lever 4 — Prompt Caching (Don't Re-Pay for the Same Instructions Every Time)

**The principle:** Every extraction call in this project will share a large, unchanging block of content: the system instructions describing the extraction task, the full schema definitions for all node types, and possibly a few worked examples showing correct extraction. Anthropic's prompt caching feature allows this shared, unchanging content to be cached on the provider's servers; a cache read costs only ten percent of the normal input token price — a ninety percent reduction — with the break-even point reached after as few as one or two reuses of that cached content.

**Applied to this project:** Structure every extraction prompt so that the large, constant part (system instructions plus the full schema) comes first and is marked as cacheable, and the small, variable part (the specific paragraph or table row being extracted in that particular call) comes last. Because this project will make many extraction calls that all share the identical instructions and schema, and differ only in which small chunk of source text is being processed, this is close to the ideal use case for caching — high reuse of a stable prefix is precisely the condition under which caching delivers its largest savings.

**Stacking the two discounts:** Batch processing and prompt caching discounts apply independently and stack together. A cached batch request becomes even cheaper because batch cuts eligible input pricing by 50% on top of the already-discounted cache read rate. Combining both levers on the same workload is the single highest-leverage engineering decision available for this project's cost profile.

## 7.6 Putting the Four Levers Together: The Pipeline Architecture

```
                         ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                         │   STATIC, CACHED PREFIX           │
                         │   (sent once, reused many times)  │
                         │                                    │
                         │  - System instructions             │
                         │  - Full node-type tool schemas     │
                         │    (from §3.4)                     │
                         │  - 2-3 worked extraction examples  │
                         └─────────────────────────────────┘
                                       │
                                       │  (cache write: paid once,
                                       │   at a small premium)
                                       ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  FOR EACH SOURCE DOCUMENT / TABLE ROW / PARAGRAPH:    │
        │                                                        │
        │   1. Append the small, variable chunk of source text  │
        │      to the cached prefix (cache read: 90% cheaper)   │
        │   2. Route to Haiku-tier model for simple, pattern-   │
        │      matchable records (most records)                 │
        │   3. Route to Sonnet-tier model only for records       │
        │      flagged ambiguous, contradictory, or low-         │
        │      confidence by a simple heuristic check             │
        │   4. Force structured tool-call output                │
        │      (guarantees valid, schema-conforming JSON)        │
        │   5. Bundle ALL of the above into ONE Batch API         │
        │      submission (50% off everything, stacks with       │
        │      caching)                                          │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                       │
                                       ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                         │  AUTOMATED VALIDATION (no LLM)    │
                         │  - Schema conformance check        │
                         │    (Pydantic, free, no tokens)     │
                         │  - Referential integrity check     │
                         │    (from §3.5, step 5)             │
                         │  - Flag any record with a          │
                         │    confidence_low marker            │
                         └─────────────────────────────────┘
                                       │
                                       ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                         │  HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP REVIEW          │
                         │  (the only step requiring a person) │
                         │  - Review only flagged/low-        │
                         │    confidence records, NOT every   │
                         │    record                          │
                         │  - Resolve contested claims per    │
                         │    §3.5 step 4 (record both,        │
                         │    don't silently pick one)         │
                         └─────────────────────────────────┘
```

This architecture is "semi-automated" in the precise sense requested: every record passes through the LLM extraction step unattended, but a human only opens the result when the automated validation step has already flagged a specific reason to look — a low-confidence score, a referential integrity failure, or a direct contradiction between two sources. This means human attention scales with the *number of actual problems in the data*, not with the *total number of records processed* — which is the entire point of semi-automation as distinct from either full manual labor or full unsupervised automation.

## 7.7 Estimated Cost Under This Architecture

**[ESTIMATE]** The following is a rough order-of-magnitude calculation, not a guaranteed quote, intended only to demonstrate the relative scale of savings from the architecture above versus a naive (unoptimized) approach. Assume the literature base for this project (per §3.2 and the sources already identified in earlier discussion) comprises on the order of 15–25 source documents, each contributing somewhere between a handful and a few dozen extractable records, for a total **[ESTIMATE] in the range of 150–400 individual entity/relationship records** to be extracted.

| Approach | Mechanism | Rough relative cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Naive baseline** | Every record sent as a separate, uncached, real-time (non-batch) call to a flagship model, full instructions repeated every time | 1x (reference point) |
| **+ Model routing only** | Cheap model for most records, flagship only for flagged ambiguous cases | roughly 0.3–0.5x of baseline |
| **+ Batch processing** | All calls submitted as a batch job | roughly 0.5x of whatever the prior step cost (the discount is unconditional and stacks) |
| **+ Prompt caching** | Shared instructions/schema cached and reused across all calls | an additional roughly 0.5–0.9x reduction on the input-token portion specifically, depending on how large the shared prefix is relative to the per-record variable text |
| **All four levers combined** | Full architecture in §7.6 | **[ESTIMATE]** plausibly in the range of 10–25% of the naive baseline cost, consistent with the general finding that strategic optimization commonly cuts LLM costs by 60–80% and that combining caching with batch discounts can push effective cost down to roughly five to ten percent of an unoptimized baseline for highly repetitive extraction workloads |

In absolute terms, given that this project's total record count is small (low hundreds, not the tens-of-thousands-per-day production workloads referenced in most published cost case studies), the realistic absolute dollar cost of the entire extraction phase under this architecture is **[ESTIMATE] likely under $5–$10 total** in raw API spend, even using a mid-tier model for the majority of calls — meaning the engineering effort invested in this architecture is justified primarily by *workflow discipline and reproducibility*, not by the absolute dollar savings alone, since the project's data volume is simply too small for the dollar amounts to be large in either the optimized or unoptimized case.

**[RECOMMENDATION]** Given the above, the practical advice is: implement model routing (§7.2) and structured output (§7.3) unconditionally, since they cost nothing extra to build and directly improve reliability regardless of project size. Implement batch processing (§7.4) and prompt caching (§7.5) as well, since both are simple configuration choices in the Anthropic API client, not architectural overhauls — there is no scenario at this project's scale where skipping them is the better choice, since they add engineering effort measured in single-digit lines of code, not added complexity that would offset their (admittedly small, in absolute dollar terms) benefit.

## 7.8 What "Semi-Automated" Explicitly Does Not Mean Here

To avoid ambiguity for future reference: this architecture does not remove the human verification requirement already established in §3.5, step 2, which states that every machine-extracted record must be spot-checked against the original source text before being accepted into the dataset, because language models can mis-state specific facts even when surrounding context is summarized correctly. The automation described in this Part 5 changes *how much human time is spent per record* and *how that time is allocated* (concentrated on flagged, uncertain records rather than spread evenly across all records) — it does not eliminate human verification as a step, because doing so would violate the scientific integrity requirement already established as non-negotiable earlier in this proposal.
